posts.title: The quiet return of the personal website
posts.excerpt: Tired of feeds they don’t control, writers and artists are going back to a page with their own name on it.
posts.content:
For a decade the advice was simple: go where the audience is. Post on the platforms, grow the follower count, and let the algorithm do the rest. Then the algorithms changed, and changed again, and a lot of people noticed that the audience had never really been theirs.

What they are building instead looks a lot like 2005. A home page. A list of posts. An about page with a photo that is not quite current. An email address, sometimes a newsletter, almost never a comment section.

Small, slow and owned

“I wanted one place where the work lives, in order, for as long as I pay the bill,” says Lena Hart, an illustrator who moved her portfolio off two social apps last spring. Her traffic is a fraction of what it was. Her commissions are up.

The feed rewards whatever you posted in the last hour. A website rewards the thing you made five years ago.

Lena Hart

Hosting is cheap, the tools are friendlier than they have ever been, and readers who arrive by a link tend to stay. None of this will replace the platforms. It does not have to. It only has to be the place you can always be found.

posts.title: What the deep-sea survey actually found
posts.excerpt: Five thousand new species made the headlines. The more interesting finding was how little we knew to look for.
posts.content:
The headline number was irresistible: more than five thousand species never described before, pulled from a stretch of Pacific sea floor the size of a small country. The survey team was more cautious than the coverage.

Most of the new species are tiny, known from a single specimen, and will take taxonomists years to name properly. What struck the researchers was not the count but the pattern: life on the abyssal plain is patchy, slow and easy to break.

Why it matters now

The same plain sits on top of metal-rich nodules that mining companies would like to lift. Recovery from a test dredge in the 1970s is still not complete. The survey gives regulators, for the first time, a baseline to measure against.

  • Fewer than one in ten samples matched a known species.
  • Many animals live attached to the nodules themselves.
  • Test tracks from decades ago are still visible on the sea floor.

“We are not saying never,” one of the authors told us. “We are saying: look first, and know what you are about to change.”

posts.title: Against the productivity gospel
posts.excerpt: An essay on the apps, rituals and morning routines that promised us more time — and what they took instead.
posts.content:
Somewhere in my phone there is an app that tracks how many glasses of water I drink, another that tracks my focus in twenty-five-minute blocks, and a third that tracks whether I have used the other two. I am, by any measure the apps understand, extremely productive. I am also tired in a way a nap does not fix.

The problem with optimising a life

Productivity advice treats time as a container to be packed more tightly. But the best hours of most lives are the unpacked ones: the walk that ran long, the conversation that went somewhere unplanned, the afternoon with nothing in it.

A calendar with no empty squares is not a sign of a full life. It is a sign of a life with no room left.

This is not an argument for doing nothing. It is an argument for choosing a few things worth doing well, and letting the rest stay undone without a notification to remind you.

posts.title: Inside the repair-café movement
posts.excerpt: Every second Saturday, volunteers with soldering irons and sewing machines fix what the manufacturers won’t.
posts.content:
The queue starts forming before ten. A toaster that clicks but will not heat. A lamp with a frayed cord. A child’s ride-on tractor, missing a wheel, carried in by a very serious four-year-old.

Behind the folding tables are retired electricians, a bike mechanic, two tailors and a software developer who learned to solder from videos during the pandemic. They fix about seven in ten of the things that come through the door.

The right to repair, in practice

New rules in several countries now require manufacturers to sell spare parts and publish repair manuals. The volunteers say the change is real but slow: glued cases and proprietary screws are still common.

Still, the mood at the tables is cheerful. “Nobody comes here angry,” says the organiser. “They come here hopeful. And most of them leave with the thing working.”

posts.title: Our critics’ year in music
posts.excerpt: Twelve albums, three arguments and one song we could not stop playing. The year, as heard by our critics.
posts.content:
It was a year of long albums and short attention spans, of debuts that sounded like greatest-hits records and veterans who finally sounded young. Our three critics agreed on almost nothing, which is how we like it.

The ones we agreed on

A slow, strange folk record made in a converted church. A dance album that is secretly about grief. A jazz trio from Lisbon who play like they are finishing each other’s sentences.

The ones we fought about

The year’s biggest pop record split the room: brilliant production, one critic said; a perfume advert with a drum machine, said another. Read both reviews and decide for yourself.

Great records do not have to be liked by everyone. They have to be impossible to ignore.

posts.title: The city that cooled its streets
posts.excerpt: White roofs, more trees and a lot of patience: how one city took four degrees off its hottest afternoons.
posts.content:
Ten years ago the city’s planners drew a map of its hottest blocks and found that it matched, almost street for street, the map of its poorest. Then they started painting.

Reflective roofs came first, because they were cheap. Trees came next, because they were slow: a street tree takes a decade to throw real shade. Finally the city opened up paved schoolyards and car parks and let the ground breathe again.

What the sensors show

On the hottest afternoons, the treated neighbourhoods now run up to four degrees cooler than they did. Hospital admissions during heatwaves are down. The trees, the planners say, are only halfway grown.

Other cities are copying the plan. The lesson they keep repeating is the least exciting one: start early, and keep going.
